Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A needles/medical visual trigger is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is clear trauma-related medical treatment, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in threat, memory, appraisals, or strategies. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal danger and intrusion rather than medical trauma cues, so this trigger appears clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid site of the event' is difficult to interpret coherently for ongoing or domestic partner abuse in this profile. If the abuse occurred in shared/home spaces, the profile would usually show corresponding location-specific triggers or avoidance themes; instead the threat items focus on general vigilance and home intrusion, making this item feel insufficiently anchored to the rest of the selected content.

vignette: Kiran Patel, a 24‑year‑old painter of South‑Eastern Asian heritage, began canvasing fresh murals on the gallery wall when his world turned sideways. A few months earlier, his girlfriend had pushed him hard enough that a bruised cheek and a sudden, electric fear became the first page of a trauma diary he never intended to keep. The night she slammed the door and slammed his head into the table, he fled, swearing that the sound of the house creaking at night would always echo his nightmare. Ever since, Kiran reports intrusive thoughts of that night that come unbidden, an ever‑present uncertainty about his safety, and a chronic sense that somebody is watching him even when he is alone in his studio. Those intrusive thoughts and that feeling of being watched have driven Kiran to develop a host of coping strategies. He refuses to go to bed unless he can turn the lights on, and when he tries to sleep he freezes at the first rustle of a chair. The fear of the unseen has also pushed him to avoid any place or time that might remind him of the assault; he keeps his tools in a locked chest and avoids the subway during rush hour. The very act of entering a room triggers an automatic scan for exits, a habit that has become his default every time he steps into a new space. When a thought surfaces, a flood of the assault’s image rushes through him, making the memory feel vivid and unending. Kiran’s internal narrative is steeped in self‑blame. He insists the night’s violence happened because of the “kind of person” he is, and this belief magnifies his sense of threat: he feels that any corner could conceal an imminent danger. The shame of being perceived as weak fuels the intrusive thoughts, which feel like constant surveillance. His guilt also paints the memory of that night as more relentless, as if the violence never truly stopped, making his sense of inadequacy grow sharper each time he recalls it. Whenever Kiran brings the assault to mind, the sudden clarity of the blow intermingles with the gaps in his timeline, and a surge of panic takes hold. The fragmented recollection feeds his conviction that he is still trapped and unworthy, reinforcing the belief that he belongs nowhere. The recollection also triggers the sensation that everyday noises could be the attacker returning, making ordinary sounds feel like looming threats. That heightened sense of danger forces him to freeze, to keep from dreaming, and to shun anything that might remind him of the attacker. The constant scanning and sense that a threat lingers in every hallway drive Kiran to avoid dreaming entirely. The relentless alertness forces him to replay the assault in his mind, reinforcing the memory with each rehearsal. He becomes convinced that his perceived inadequacy is real, that he can never feel safe. The ever‑present danger amplifies the intrusive thoughts that come as if someone is watching him, even in silence. By staying away from any dream, by freezing whenever a spark of fear ignites, Kiran never processes the event, keeping the memory fragmented. The avoidance also cements his belief that he is fundamentally flawed. Each time he evades a reminder, the urge to stay vigilant strengthens, making the intrusive thoughts feel even more intrusive. The avoidance also heightens his threat perception, making him scan even the quietest corners. Today Kiran sits before his easel, brush poised but trembling, feeling the weight of every brushstroke as a test of his vigilance. He finally seeks help because the cycle has grown too tight: he cannot sleep, he fears being watched in his own apartment, and he longs for a way to regain control over his mind and his life.
